items.title: Burnout syndrome among education professionals: challenges for well-being and teaching performance
items.abstract: Burnout syndrome is one of the leading occupational health problems currently affecting education professionals and represents a growing challenge to the quality and sustainability of educational systems. The objective of this article was to analyze burnout syndrome among teachers through a literature review of recent scientific evidence, examining its conceptual foundations, risk factors, consequences for well-being and professional performance, as well as the main prevention and intervention strategies. The literature search was conducted using international scientific databases and publications from specialized organizations, with priority given to studies published between 2018 and 2026. The reviewed evidence demonstrates that burnout is a multidimensional phenomenon arising from the interaction of high job demands, insufficient organizational support, administrative overload, limited opportunities for professional development, and work-life imbalance. Furthermore, the findings indicate that teacher burnout negatively affects mental health, job satisfaction, professional commitment, teaching quality, and educational outcomes. The studies analyzed consistently show that interventions focused exclusively on the individual are insufficient unless accompanied by structural changes within educational institutions. Consequently, burnout prevention requires comprehensive policies that combine the strengthening of personal resources with organizational strategies aimed at improving working conditions, promoting teacher well-being, and fostering higher-quality and more sustainable education.

items.title: Changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions of an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway: a longitudinal empirical ethics survey
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-supported learning is increasingly used in medical education, including doctor–patient communication training. Such systems may provide virtual dialogue practice, immediate structured feedback, reflection prompts and opportunities for further practice after feedback. However, educational usefulness does not necessarily imply ethical acceptability. This study examined changes in medical students’ ethical and acceptability-related perceptions before and after participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway. This longitudinal empirical ethics survey was nested within a course-based randomised educational trial but was analytically independent of the parent trial’s educational outcome analysis. Surveys were administered after random allocation to the AI-supported pathway but before exposure to AI-supported learning functions (T0), at the end of the 8-week course (T1), and at the 3-month follow-up (T2). The main analysis focused on students in the AI-supported pathway with complete T0–T1–T2 ethics-related scale data and analysable T2 open-text responses ( n = 31). The open-text question was included only at T2. The primary comparison was the within-participant T0–T2 change across six ethics-related domains. Two domains showed statistically significant T0–T2 changes. Trust in AI feedback decreased from 3.86 (0.55) to 3.20 (0.62), with a mean change of − 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] − 0.88 to − 0.42), Cohen’s d z = − 1.04 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. Room to question AI outputs increased from 2.71 (0.68) to 3.67 (0.58), with a mean change of 0.96 (95% CI 0.69 to 1.23), Cohen’s d z = 1.29 and Holm–Bonferroni-adjusted p < 0.001. The remaining four domains showed small, non-significant changes after Holm–Bonferroni correction. T2 open-text responses indicated that students recognised the formative value of AI feedback while emphasising critical use, teacher supervision, preservation of interpersonal interaction and clearer data governance. This exploratory longitudinal empirical ethics survey showed that, following participation in an AI-supported doctor–patient communication learning pathway, two of the six ethics-related domains showed statistically significant changes: trust in AI feedback decreased, while perceived room to question AI outputs increased. These findings support continued attention to ethics-focused evaluation and clear governance arrangements in AI-supported learning pathways.

items.abstract: The study examines the growing presence of generative artificial intelligence in education and focuses on teachers' perceptions of ChatGPT as a support tool in the teaching and learning process. The development of AI is transforming teaching practices by enabling content personalisation, the creation of educational materials, and more efficient lesson preparation; at the same time, it raises questions about the reliability of generated content, ethical considerations, and teachers' digital competencies. In the context of the specific characteristics of the Polish education system—an ageing workforce, the feminisation of the profession, and the outflow of young teachers—the implementation of technological innovations may be uneven. The study aims to explore teachers’ familiarity with ChatGPT, its use in their daily practice, and the barriers and concerns associated with its adoption. The findings contribute to the discussion on the responsible integration of AI in education and indicate directions for teachers’ professional development.

items.title: Christian Educators’ Response to Possible Effects of Excessive Dependence on Artificial Intelligence Tools on Youths’ Mental Health
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has a significant influence on various aspects of human life. While there are numerous benefits from utilising AI tools, excessive dependence on them in education raises concerns, especially with regard to youth mental health. This study examines the possible effects of overreliance on Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on youth mental health. It explores the role of Christian educators in addressing these challenges. The paper provides an overview of mental health by emphasising its multifaceted nature and encompassing emotional, psychological, cognitive, and social well-being. The paper argues that although AI tools have revolutionised education and have led to improvements and productivity, their overuse among young people raises concerns about mental health implications. Such mental health implications include diminished critical thinking, reduced autonomy, impaired memory skills, and social isolation. Moreover, the paper highlights the role of Christian educators in addressing the excessive usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools. The strategies proposed for combating the concern are AI literacy, curriculum development, mental health awareness, and promoting balanced learning approaches. As Christian educators integrate biblical principles and responsible AI use, the negative effect of AI overdependence among youth will be alleviated.

items.title: Clinical Feedback as a Relational and Organisational Process: A Qualitative Study of Students’ Experiences in Operating Room Environment
items.abstract: Background: Clinical feedback is central to workplace learning in operating room education. While clinical feedback has been conceptualised as relational and context-dependent, less is known about how Operating Room Technology students perceive and experience it within the operating room learning environment. Methods: A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with 17 Operating Room Technology students recruited through maximum variation purposive sampling from Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Data were collected between November 2025 and March 2026 and analysed using Graneheim and Lundman’s inductive content analysis. Trustworthiness was addressed using Lincoln and Guba’s criteria. Results: Five themes comprising 13 subcategories were identified: structural and executive framework of clinical feedback; perceived consequences of clinical feedback quality; harmful feedback practices and barriers; interaction and professionalism in feedback; and individual and professional competencies of instructors in feedback. Students described clinical feedback as most valuable when it was structured, timely, respectful, and dialogic, and perceived it as contributing to confidence, engagement, and professional identity. Delayed, vague, or humiliating clinical feedback was perceived to undermine confidence and psychological safety. Divergent accounts highlighted tensions between immediate intra-operative clinical feedback and workflow demands, as well as circumstances in which public safety-critical corrections were perceived as necessary. Conclusions: The findings suggest that clinical feedback in Operating Room Technology education is a multidimensional process perceived to be shaped by structural, relational, organisational, and educator-related factors. Rather than proposing a new conceptualisation, this study provides a context-specific understanding of how established clinical feedback principles are perceived and negotiated within the operating room learning environment. Strengthening educator capabilities, embedding structured clinical feedback approaches, and fostering psychologically safe learning environments may strengthen clinical education in Operating Room Technology programmes. Keywords: clinical feedback, workplace learning, operating room learning environment, psychological safety, feedback practices

items.title: Communication facilitates focused monitoring and anticipation of critical events: evidence from eye movements
items.abstract: The present study investigates the impact of communication availability on monitoring behaviour in a team. A monitoring task was designed to compare participants who were not allowed to communicate with those allowed to communicate while monitoring an automated system and deciding repeatedly whether critical events would turn into failures. Four monitoring phases were distinguished around every critical event: identification, verification, anticipation, and detection. Eye-tracking parameters obtained during these phases were related to relevant areas of interest. Results show that the opportunity to communicate increases the proportion of attention on relevant events, particularly during anticipation, and leads to faster fixations on failures during detection.

items.title: Confident but absent: AI use, self-efficacy for independent learning, and student absenteeism in higher education
items.abstract: Rising student absenteeism remains a persistent challenge in higher education, potentially exacerbated by the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools. Drawing on digital displacement theory, this study examines whether general AI use is associated with students’ self-efficacy for independent learning and absenteeism. Survey data from 291 Portuguese university students were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, explaining 38.7% of the variance in absenteeism and 34.4% in self-efficacy. Internal locus of control, peer influence, time management, and AI use emerged as significant predictors. General AI use was positively associated with both self-efficacy and absenteeism, suggesting that AI may strengthen independent learning confidence while coinciding with reduced face-to-face engagement. Multigroup analysis provided exploratory evidence of gender differences, with the AI use–self-efficacy relationship stronger among males at the 5% level, while other gender differences appeared only at a more lenient 10% threshold.

items.title: Connectedness, Cognitive Load, and Human-AI Oversight in Cyber Operations
items.abstract: AI-assisted cyber situational awareness triggers machine-generated reasoning traces (step-by-step justifications for anomaly classifications) that a human operator is expected to review. Because cyber signals and their traces arrive faster than any operator can process, human review is the limiting constraint on oversight. The standard approach is to identify the riskiest cyber events for review using model-side signals such as confidence or uncertainty. That framing ignores the operator's cognitive capacity which varies sharply with the operational environment. We propose an alternative where the system's environmental and connectivity telemetry serves as an available, non-invasive proxy for operator load. That same telemetry determines whether the human-AI partnership can reach the broader collective for support. In a maritime platform, environmental and connectivity attributes including depth, number of active communications paths, density of the tracked contact picture, and operational tempo all carry this signal. Need for operator oversight becomes a decision that materializes as a combination of both risk and environment-derived operator capacity. We present a reference architecture for a connectedness-aware oversight engine, demonstrating everyday use cases alongside its intended incorporation into the submarine cyber-defense toolkit. Two themes emerge: 1) the operator's environmental state is itself a connectedness measurement, and 2) connectedness drives the cognitive load and defines a collective boundary in human-AI cyber operations.

items.title: Current State of AI in Surgery and Anesthesiology Selected Applications, Limits, and a Responsible Agenda for Latin America
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in surgery and anesthesiology encompasses different tasks: risk prediction, hypotension alerts, video analysis, technical-skill assessment, surgical-duration estimation, and postoperative support. Treating them as one promise of “AI surgery” obscures essential distinctions among retrospective performance, external validation, prospective clinical utility, impact on processes or outcomes, and routine implementation. This whitepaper synthesizes selected applications rather than exhaustively cataloguing all subspecialties, robotic platforms, or simulation techniques. The evidence closest to clinical evaluation in anesthesiology is concentrated in intraoperative hypotension prediction. A systematic review and meta-analysis included eight randomized-trial reports; its published total of 568 participants includes overlap between a study and its substudy and does not represent unique individuals. Seven reports evaluated the Hypotension Prediction Index and one evaluated fuzzy-logic control. The hypotension meta-analysis including the largest trial did not find a statistically significant difference and showed high heterogeneity. Favorable results from small trials do not establish universal benefit: this is a narrow family of systems, populations, and protocols. In surgery, phase recognition and technical-skill assessment have systematic reviews, whereas models for complications, delirium, length of stay, and surgical duration remain dominated by retrospective development or limited validation. Latin America has direct evidence that should not be replaced by silent extrapolation. A Bogotá study evaluated models for surgical-duration estimation; Brazilian studies developed models for postoperative delirium and length of stay after coronary artery bypass grafting; and LASOS described perioperative outcomes across 17 countries. These sources demonstrate regional research and data capacity and a measurable perioperative burden; they do not demonstrate general clinical effectiveness of AI, routine implementation, or transportability across countries. The directed search identified few regional AI records compared with the international literature; statements about infrastructure, interoperability, and governance therefore also rely on regional sources and are labelled as implementation context or inference, not model performance. Central finding: AI can currently support bounded perioperative surveillance, prediction, analysis, training, and operational tasks. It cannot yet responsibly promise independent intraoperative decisions, replacement of surgical or anesthetic

items.title: Designing healthy and resilient information environments: A multi‐agent sandbox for exploring risks and countermeasures
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is transforming online information environments, amplifying both societal benefits and risks. This article argues that online platforms can be understood as multi‐agent systems (MAS) composed of humans, simulated users, adversarial agents, and defensive agents operating under platform‐level rules. In this MAS‐based framework, persuasion, trust, coordination, and governance interact to shape system‐level outcomes. To study these dynamics safely, we introduce a sandbox environment in which human participants, red bots, green bots, and blue bots can be observed under controlled conditions. Early experiences with the sandbox show that persuasive agents can be built with little effort, that current large language model (LLM) agents lack psychological realism, and that humans may struggle to distinguish malicious red bots from benign participants. The sandbox enables stakeholders to experience and evaluate trade‐offs in moderation, amplification, and intervention strategies. We outline a research agenda for improving agent validity, modelling advanced threats, and designing human–machine teams that support healthier, more resilient information environments.

items.title: Designing Trust, Autonomy, and Acceptance in AI-Based Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Comparative Experimental Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems (AI CDSS) have the potential to improve clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, yet their adoption remains limited. Prior research highlights trust in AI and concerns about professional autonomy as key barriers to implementation. While explainability and system integration may foster trust, they may simultaneously threaten professional identity and decision authority. At the same time, perceived usefulness has been identified as the central driver of technology acceptance, although it is shaped by autonomyrelated concerns, particularly among physicians. This study integrates two experimental investigations (1,2) to examine how AI-CDSS design features jointly influence trust, autonomy-related perceptions, and acceptance across patients and physicians. Methods: The analysis combines and compares findings from two vignette-based experimental studies. The first study (n = 292) employs a 2 × 2 × 2 factorial design manipulating AI explainability, workflow integration, and accountability to assess their effects on trust and professional identity threat among physicians. The second study consists of three experiments across patients (n = 209), potential future users (n = 1062), and physicians (n = 185), manipulating AI-CDSS system type (hybrid vs. autonomous) and recommendation risk (lifestyle vs. medical) (2 x 2 factorial design). Regression-based mediation and sequential mediation models (SPSS PROCESS Macro) were applied using bootstrapping procedures. Results: Results from the first study show that explainability and workflow integration significantly increase trust in AI-CDSS. At the same time, explainability and system-induced accountability increase perceived professional identity threat. Trust is negatively associated with identity threat and partially mediates the relationship between explainability and identity threat, indicating that trust can mitigate but not fully offset these concerns. Results from the second study demonstrate that perceived usefulness is the strongest predictor of intention to use among both patients, potential future users, and physicians. However, the underlying mechanisms differ. Patients and potential future users evaluate AI-CDSS primarily based on perceived usefulness, whereas physicians’ evaluations depend on professional autonomy preservation. For physicians, hybrid systems increase intention to use only indirectly through reduced professional autonomy concerns and increased perceived usefulness. High-risk medical recommendations consistently increase perceived or anticipated professional autonomy concerns across all groups but do not directly reduce perceived usefulness or intention to use. Conclusion: AI-CDSS acceptance is shaped by the interplay of trust, perceived usefulness, and professional autonomy-related concerns. Design features exhibit ambivalent effects, simultaneously enabling and constraining adoption. Successful implementation requires aligning system design with professional expectations, particularly by preserving physician decision authority while demonstrating clear clinical value.

items.title: Detecting and Mitigating Bias in AI Systems: A Methodological Approach to Social Inequality
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly embedded in decisions that affect health, employment, housing, justice, and social policy. Rather than neutral tools, they reflect the data on which they are trained, the objectives they optimize, and the contexts in which they operate, reinforcing and amplifying existing social inequalities. This paper addresses two interrelated questions: how can we detect bias across the AI lifecycle, and what technical and governance strategies can effectively mitigate it? Drawing on critical social science perspectives, empirical case studies from healthcare, housing, policing, and labor markets, and recent advances in fair machine learning (including causal debiasing, synthetic data generation, and fair representation learning), the paper develops a conceptual framework, grounded in sociological theories, spanning data collection, preprocessing, model training, deployment, and post-deployment monitoring. As an original contribution, the paper proposes two complementary analytical frameworks: a Social Harm-Intervention Mapping that recasts mitigation strategies in terms of the types of inequality they address, and an Accountability Matrix that maps agency and accountability gaps across social actors and pipeline stages. The paper argues that these frameworks provide social researchers and policymakers with more actionable guidance than conventional pipeline taxonomies because they foreground the social and institutional dimensions of AI-induced inequality rather than treating bias as a purely technical problem.

items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has brought pedagogical opportunities to the fore, but it has also made students’ affective responses, particularly concern related to AI usage, more visible. The aim of this study is to develop the Educational Artificial Intelligence Use Concerns Scale within the framework of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and AI concern and anxiety literature. The scale development process was conducted using the classical test theory approach and included the following stages: item pool creation, content validity through expert opinion, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), and reliability-validity analyses. Data were collected from higher education students enrolled at [name of university / universities] in [city, country] through an online survey distributed via [institutional e-mail / classroom announcements / learning management system / social media], and separate samples were used for EFA (n = 300) and CFA (n = 129). CFA results yielded a two-factor structure, explaining 57.99% of the total variance. CFA findings revealed that the twofactor structure showed acceptable/excellent fit (χ²/df=1.88; CFI=.98; TLI=.98; RMSEA=.08; SRMR=.01). The scale’s internal consistency was found to be high (total α = .90), and convergent validity was supported by AVE values. The results indicate that the scale is a valid and reliable tool for measuring concerns related to AI use in higher education contexts. The scale can contribute to studies explaining the acceptance and integration of AI in education, particularly when used in conjunction with TAM variables, by examining the role of affective determinants in technology acceptance processes.

items.title: Digital Dependency and Academic Identity Among Postgraduate Students in the Era of Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has become embedded in everyday university life, often faster than institutional guidance has developed. This qualitative hermeneutic phenomenological study examined how postgraduate students experienced the boundary between generative-AI assistance and digital dependency, and how these experiences related to academic identity. In-depth, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eleven postgraduate students (five males and six females) at a public university in Saudi Arabia, selected through maximum-variation purposive sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and returned to participants for verification. Analysis followed Van Manen’s holistic, selective, and detailed approaches to phenomenological reflection. Two themes captured the experience: negotiating the boundary of digital dependency, and academic identity between agency and dependence. Rather than locating dependency in frequency of use, participants located it in the recurring transfer of substantive ideation, judgment, and authorship to the tool. Verification and the ability to explain and defend the final work helped preserve epistemic agency, whereas time pressure sometimes shifted practice toward substitution. Within this sample, strategic use as a coach, critic, or organizer supported confidence and skill development; extensive delegation was associated in participants’ accounts with diminished ownership, guilt, and concealment-oriented assessment practices. The findings offer a provisional, sample-grounded account of digital dependency and suggest that perceived ambiguity in institutional expectations may make concealment more salient, without establishing a causal relationship.

items.title: Digital Transformation and the Future of Higher Education: A Comprehensive Umbrella Review
items.abstract: Digital transformation (DT) is fundamentally changing the higher education institutions (HEIs) around the globe. The COVID-19 pandemic has drastically increased using digitally enabled approaches for teaching, learning, research, and administration, driven by the convergence of technologies encompassing the industry 4.0. Despite the various existing reviews that tackle digital transformation separately, some, such as those on the technology adoption or strategic planning, or pedagogical innovation, have limited scope and do not offer an overall, multi-dimensional synthesis. This rather comprehensive umbrella review combines dimensions, technologies, strategic processes and actors related to the implementation of DT in HEIs, based on the systematic and multivocal literature reviews, analyses via PRISMA, and thematic synthesises of articles, published from 2015 to 2024, in Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Springer Link and ACM Digital Library databases. A total of 47 studies in the analytical corpus, two of which were anchor reviews and 43 were complementary primary studies, were identified in an initial pool of 312 records. The findings showed that most digital transformation projects (DTIs) in the education sector are concentrated on competitive education (24%) and that the dominant enabling technologies are analytics (23%), cloud computing (20%), and artificial intelligence (16%). Most of all, just one-quarter of HEIs can speak with any degree of fluency about a digital strategy and only 56% of DTIs are part of a broader institutional agenda. The review concludes that, based on the importance of those topics in the curriculum, student demand satisfaction (12%) and digital culture (9%) fall short of expected levels of investment. The results are derived from the existing reviews and primary studies and thus share the limitations of the primary literature reviewed. The results highlight the need for university leaders to create digital strategies that are integrated, invest in faculty development and digital culture, and embrace a transformative approach instead of a technology-only approach to the implementation of digital transformation.
